claims.text: As-rolled Q235 steel in its untreated pre-exposure state possesses a naturally formed protective oxide layer.
The naturally formed oxide layer governs the onset or suppression of corrosion in Q235 steel under chloride-rich harsh environments.
At room temperature, the oxide layer remains compact.
A compact oxide layer limits corrosive attack on Q235 steel.
Elevated temperature degrades the oxide film by increasing its porosity or defect density.
Degradation of the oxide film accelerates localized corrosion.
Slow oxidation kinetics at room temperature produce a coherent, compact oxide layer.
The coherent, compact oxide layer reduces ingress of corrosive species.
Faster oxidation at elevated temperature promotes formation of a less adherent, porous oxide film.
At room temperature, the treated samples will have lower weight loss and fewer pits than the untreated samples.
At elevated temperature, oxide-film degradation will produce more localized corrosion than in the reference.
At elevated temperature, Q235 steel will exhibit a higher overall corrosion rate than the reference.
The proposed temperature-dependent oxide-film mechanism applies within a moderate elevated-temperature range under chloride-rich conditions with controlled pH and humidity.
Changes in electrolyte composition or extreme temperature or humidity may alter oxide-film behavior and corrosion dynamics.

contradictions.description: The nominal test samples and untreated baseline are both described as untreated Q235 steel exposed to the same chloride-rich environment. No distinct room-temperature treatment is defined, yet the prediction asserts lower corrosion for 'treated samples' relative to the untreated samples.

The hypothesis attributes protection to the naturally formed oxide film, whereas the experiment optionally substitutes a pre-induced controlled oxide film. Such a film may differ in composition, thickness, and formation history, so this arm does not cleanly test the stated natural-film mechanism.

The elevated-temperature prediction refers to increased corrosion relative to an undefined 'reference,' while the baseline is said to be exposed to the same environment. It is unclear whether the reference is the room-temperature group or an untreated group at the same elevated temperature.
